questions.q: Why does this lab harden Conditional Access and IAM policy before touching the NSG and Security Group rules?
options: Network changes must always be approved by a change board first
A valid, overly permissive credential walks straight through a tightened network boundary, so identity has to be fixed first
Azure requires NSGs to be configured before Conditional Access can be enabled
AWS Security Groups cannot be edited until an IAM Access Analyzer scan completes
questions.explain: Tightening the network doesn't help if an attacker already holds a credential with wide IAM or RBAC permissions -- identity is hardened first for that reason.

questions.q: Why does the lab run the new Conditional Access policy in Report-only mode before switching it to On?
options: Report-only is the only mode Entra ID supports for admin accounts
Report-only mode automatically grants MFA exemptions
It disables all other Conditional Access policies while active
It logs what the policy would have blocked without actually blocking anyone, so unexpected impact can be caught before go-live
questions.explain: A Report-only run surfaces what the policy would have done against real sign-ins first, catching unintended blocks before the policy actually enforces anything.

questions.q: In the AWS IAM step, why does the lab delete the old wildcard policy and write a new scoped one, rather than just adding a Deny statement on top?
options: A Deny statement is functionally identical to deleting the Allow, so it doesn't matter which is used
AWS does not support Deny statements in IAM policies
Replacing the wildcard Action/Resource grant with the exact actions and ARNs the role's real traffic needs is the least-privilege rewrite the lesson is demonstrating
Deny statements can only be attached to Security Groups, not IAM roles
questions.explain: The point of the exercise is rewriting the grant itself down to only what's actually used, not layering a deny on top of an otherwise still-wildcard policy.

questions.q: After rewriting the meridian-cicd-deploy IAM policy, what does the lab use to confirm the fix actually held?
options: Re-running IAM Access Analyzer and confirming the earlier wildcard finding is gone with no new finding introduced
Manually reading every CloudTrail event for the past year
Deleting the role and recreating it from scratch
Checking the AWS billing dashboard for a cost change
questions.explain: IAM Access Analyzer surfaced the original wildcard grant as a finding; re-running it after the rewrite is the real verification step.

questions.q: Why does the lab delete the Any-to-Any NSG rule outright instead of just narrowing its source IP range in place?
options: Azure does not allow editing an existing NSG rule's source field
Deleting and re-adding costs nothing extra, while narrowing in place is somehow disallowed
A rule that is merely 'shrunk' is easy to accidentally widen again later, so replacing it with new scoped rules makes the intent explicit
NSG rules must be deleted and recreated every time the VM they protect is rebooted
questions.explain: Replacing the rule outright, rather than editing its source in place, avoids leaving a rule that someone could later 'temporarily' widen back toward Any.
